opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Michael. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay, sure. Sorry, I'm a bit tired, it's busy season. But yeah, I've got opinions on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it helps with the grunt work. Pulling invoices, matching numbers, writing up notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even this one makes me nervous, honestly. I use it every day and I can see how much of my job it already does. If it stops here, great. I just don't believe it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Study for my accounting exams like I'm supposed to. Try to get onto the bigger clients, where there's more judgement and less ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low hum of worry. That's sort of normal for me.

S0.say: It helps with the grunt work, like pulling invoices and matching numbers.
S0.think: He uses it daily and sees how much of his job it already does. He doesn't believe it will stop here.
S0.do: Studies for his accounting exams and tries to get onto bigger clients with more judgement work.
S0.feel: A low hum of worry, which is normal for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good thing I got in when I did. Half my friends from uni can't get graduate jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picked accounting because everyone said it was safe. Turns out ticking and checking is exactly what AI is best at. Slow just means I find out slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the exams no matter what, because a qualified accountant is worth more than an associate. Pay a bit extra on my student loan. Maybe look at moving into tax advice, which feels more human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I picked the wrong road.

S1.say: Good thing I got in when I did. Half my uni friends can't get graduate jobs.
S1.think: He chose accounting because it felt safe, but checking numbers is what AI is best at.
S1.do: Finishes his exams, pays a little extra on his student loan and looks at moving into tax advice.
S1.feel: Like he picked the wrong road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep quiet at work. You don't want to look scared. Online I'd say the firms should keep training grads, or there's no one to sign off audits in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep quiet at work. Would anyone there know how worried you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Maybe one friend in my team. Everyone's acting fine, so I act fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the routine office work. That's literally me. I'd be in the first round of cuts, or my pay would stall while the senior people keep theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Update my CV and apply for in-house finance jobs at companies, which feel a bit safer. Cut spending, stop eating out. Ask about putting my loan payments on hold if I lose the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach. Not sleeping great.

S2.say: Firms should keep training graduates, or there'll be no one to sign off audits in ten years.
S2.think: He is the routine office work and would be in the first round of cuts.
S2.do: Applies for in-house finance jobs, cuts spending and asks about pausing loan payments.
S2.feel: Sick in the stomach and not sleeping well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's insane that shares and houses boom while a whole generation gets locked out. I'd probably post about it, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is gone, and the qualified accountants above me are going too, so there's nowhere to climb. I have debt, no savings and no house. I don't know what I'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply for anything. Maybe a trade, because physical jobs are safe in this one, but I'd have to start from zero. I'd move back in with my parents to stop paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like everything I did was for nothing.

S3.say: It's insane that shares and houses boom while a whole generation gets locked out.
S3.think: His job is gone and so are the jobs above him. With debt and no savings, he doesn't know what he'd be.
S3.do: Applies for anything, considers starting a trade from zero and moves back in with his parents.
S3.feel: Panicky, like everything he did was for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need something like a basic income now, because there's no line of work left to tell people to go into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strangely, it's a bit less lonely. Last time it was people like me. Now it's everyone, so the government can't ignore it. That doesn't pay my loan though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay with my parents. Look for any work where people want a human, like caring or teaching. Join whatever group is pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared. A bit less alone in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that really less scary than the last one, or just different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Different. Still scary. But when it's just you, you think it's your fault. When it's everyone, it isn't.

S4.say: We need something like a basic income, because there's no line of work left to point people to.
S4.think: Now that it's everyone, the government can't ignore it, but that doesn't pay his loan.
S4.do: Stays with his parents, looks for work where people want a human and joins a group pushing for a basic income.
S4.feel: Still scared, but less alone in it.
